newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parties to battle voter apathy in polls.
newsitem.headline: Japan parties to battle voter apathy in polls.

text.p: What if Japan held an election and nobody came?

Politicians jockeying for position ahead of a looming general election could find their toughest battles are not with each other, but against an apathy which has frayed many voters' attachment to any party at all.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, in a widely expected move, told his ruling coalition partners on Thursday that he would dissolve parliament's Lower House on Friday.
Polls must be held within 40 days of a dissolution and coalition officials have said October 20 is the likely date.

The election will be the first poll for the Lower House -- the more powerful of Japan's two chambers of parliament -- since the conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) temporarily lost a nearly four-decade grip on power in July 1993. Hashimoto is now LDP president.
It is also the first test of a new electoral system which combines 300 single-member districts with 200 districts where members are selected by proportional representation.
Critics charged that the old multi-member district system stifled policy debate, favoured rural voters, fostered corruption and blocked emergence of true two-party democracy.

Wooing the masses of voters -- nearly half by many estimates -- who do not support any particular party and who may decline to cast their ballots at all will be a major challenge, though admittedly less so for politicians backed by well-oiled machines and ample funds, analysts said.
"Apathy does serve the interests of a lot of people, although they can't say that out loud," one analyst said.

The main rivals in the election are the LDP, the conservative opposition Shinshinto, and the Democratic Party, a new group led by would-be reformers which must rely mostly on rebels from the LDP's current partners, the tiny New Party Sakigake and the Social Democrats, for members.
Many pundits say the LDP is likely to win a plurality but will have to seek junior partners to form yet another coalition government. Surprises, however, could be in store.

"The most important factor is that more than 50 percent of the electorate are in no sympathy with any particular party," said Takashi Inoguchi, a political scientist at the United Nations University in Tokyo. "It's very, very volatile."
Many voters were disillusioned by machinations which followed the unravelling of an unwieldy coalition which ousted the LDP in August 1993.

That coalition delivered its promised electoral reform -- no mean feat -- but the LDP's return to power in 1994 in a ruling bloc that included its long-time rivals, the Socialists, left many dubious about prospects for meaningful change.

"In spite of all the turmoil in 1993, the LDP is back in power, and there is discontent with the reform parties, which failed to deliver a new kind of politics," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
Aware of a vague popular sentiment that old ways must be altered, politicians of every ilk are proclaiming dedication to "reform", co-opting rivals' slogans and blurring policy gaps.

Topping the list of changes everyone says they want is "administrative reform", a broad concept encompassing varying prescriptions for smaller government, more political control over policy, and fewer of the regulations critics say suffocate Japan's private sector.
One of the few areas where voters will have a clear choice is over an increase in the nation's three percent consumption tax, which is due to rise to five percent from April.

The LDP is defending the unpopular tax increase as vital given Japan's huge budget deficit and its rapidly aging population, while Shinshinto is calling for a freeze until real administrative reform and government cost-cutting takes place.
"That's an issue, but it's not exactly a vision for the nation," Neuffer said.
